title: How does nutrition change disease risk? Deficiency and excess, iron, vitamins C and D, iodine, and type 2 diabetes as a risk pattern
subtitle: A century ago, Australian children were treated for rickets and scurvy; today the nutrition-linked diseases that fill hospitals are mostly type 2 diabetes and heart disease. How does what we eat change disease risk?
subject: Biology
lessonIntent: using the chain nutrient, normal job, change, effect; distinguishing deficiency (too little for long enough that a process fails) from excess (too much over years, overloading a system); explaining iron-deficiency anaemia (less haemoglobin, less oxygen carried, fatigue on exercise); explaining scurvy (vitamin C needed to build strong collagen; weak collagen, leaky vessels, bleeding gums, slow healing) and rickets (vitamin D needed to absorb calcium; soft bones bend); explaining goitre (too little iodine, less thyroid hormone, more TSH by negative feedback, the gland grows but still lacks iodine); explaining insulin resistance (excess energy and low activity build up body fat; insulin binds but fewer transporters move; glucose stays in the blood), beta cell compensation and its failure, and vessel damage from years of high glucose; distinguishing a risk factor from a certain outcome, comparing scurvy (one missing nutrient) with type 2 diabetes and heart disease (several risk factors); applying the chain to an unseen vitamin D case and evaluating a causal claim from rate data.

voiceover.text: A century ago, Australian doctors still treated children for rickets, where growing bones soften and bend, and scurvy, where gums bleed and wounds won't heal. Today, the nutrition-linked diseases that fill our hospitals are mostly type 2 diabetes and heart disease. One set comes from too little. The other is linked to long-term excess, alongside other risk factors. So how does what we eat change disease risk?

Earlier, you saw that nutrition is one acquired cause of disease. Here's the chain that explains any case. Start with the nutrient and its normal job in the body. Then ask what changes when there's too little for long enough, a deficiency, or too much over many years, an excess. Then link that change to the effect. A deficiency takes away a job. An excess overloads a system that normally works.

Take iron. You've seen its chain already: too little iron means less haemoglobin, smaller, paler red cells, and less oxygen carried, which is iron-deficiency anaemia. The nutrition question is why the iron is low. A diet with too little iron, or a gut that absorbs it poorly, makes it a nutritional deficiency. But losing blood, for example from heavy periods or bleeding in the gut, drains iron too, and that cause isn't the diet. So check where the iron went before you call it nutritional.

The same chain works for vitamins. Vitamin C is needed by the enzymes that build strong collagen, the rope-like protein that holds together gums, skin and blood vessel walls. Without it, new collagen is weak, so small vessels leak, gums bleed and wounds heal slowly. That's scurvy. Vitamin D lets your gut absorb calcium. Without it, growing bones don't harden properly, so they can bend under the body's weight. That's rickets. Scurvy has a C in it, for vitamin C. Rickets, think vitamin D. Your skin can make it in sunlight, and some foods and supplements supply it too.

Iodine adds a twist you'll recognise from homeostasis. Your thyroid gland uses iodine to build its hormones, which set how fast your cells use energy. With too little iodine, those hormone levels fall. Negative feedback responds: the pituitary releases more TSH, thyroid-stimulating hormone, telling the thyroid to work harder, and the gland grows. But the missing ingredient is still missing, so it keeps enlarging into a goitre. That's one reason Australian bread has been made with iodised salt since 2009.

Now excess, and type 2 diabetes. Remember what insulin does: it binds to muscle and fat cells, and that signal moves glucose transporters into the membrane, so glucose gets in. Years of taking in more energy than you use, with little activity, build up body fat, especially around the liver and other organs. Muscle and fat cells then respond less to insulin. Insulin still binds, but fewer transporters move, so less glucose gets in. The liver also keeps releasing glucose when insulin should slow it down. Both keep blood glucose high. That's insulin resistance.

At first, the beta cells in the pancreas cover for it by releasing more insulin, so blood glucose can stay close to normal for years. That's why many people don't know anything's wrong. Over time, the beta cells may not keep up, and blood glucose stays high. That's type 2 diabetes. Years of high glucose damage blood vessels, from tiny ones in the eyes, kidneys and nerves to the arteries feeding the heart. When the Australian AusDiab study tested adults, about half of those with diabetes hadn't been diagnosed.

So does eating too much cause type 2 diabetes? Not on its own. Compare scurvy: one missing nutrient, and the disease follows reliably until vitamin C is restored. Type 2 diabetes is different. Excess intake is a risk factor, something that raises the chance of disease without guaranteeing it. Family history, age, activity, sleep and some medicines change the risk too, and so does what food people can afford and reach. Heart disease is similar: saturated fat can raise LDL cholesterol, which helps build the plaque you saw with smoking, but it's one risk factor among several.

Two exam questions. First. A fourteen-year-old spends almost all daylight hours indoors. Blood tests show low vitamin D, and their gut is absorbing little calcium. Using nutrient, change and effect, explain how this deficiency could affect their bones. Pause here to answer.

The nutrient is vitamin D, and its job is helping the gut absorb calcium. With little sunlight, the skin makes little vitamin D, so less calcium is absorbed. Growing bone doesn't harden properly and stays soft, so it can bend under the body's weight, which is rickets. The classic mistake is answering "drink more milk". Without vitamin D, extra calcium isn't absorbed well.

Second. The chart shows new cases of type 2 diabetes per thousand adults each year, in four groups sorted by body weight and family history. Identify two risk factors the data show. Then explain why the claim "eating too much causes type 2 diabetes" overstates the evidence. Pause here to answer.

Obesity and a family history both go with higher rates, and together, the highest. But even in the highest group, about thirty in a thousand developed diabetes each year, so most didn't, and some healthy-weight adults did. And the data didn't measure food intake, so they can't show that eating too much caused these cases. The classic mistake is treating a higher rate as a guarantee.

So for any nutrition question, name the nutrient and its normal job, say what changes with too little or too much, link it to the effect, then ask: is this one missing nutrient, or one risk factor among many? Next, what happens when cell division escapes control: how cancer begins and spreads.
